claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really uncomfortable—especially in a lab group where you *need* to explain your work. From what you describe, two things can be true at once: (1) you may genuinely have an accent/English struggle *right now* (totally normal in your first weeks/semester), and (2) your teammates’ reaction (laughter, “what?”) could feel unfair and humiliating—so your brain is understandably trying to protect you by thinking “maybe they’ve decided I can’t speak.”
claim_review_spans.R2: I can’t know the rubric or what they “decided,” but you do have options that don’t require guessing.
claim_review_spans.R3: In group projects, task lists often start as “default roles” (who prepares what first), not final speaking assignments. Also, teammates sometimes assume someone is less confident instead of checking. Since your presentation is soon, you need a quick, low-risk clarification.
claim_review_spans.R4: You’re not asking “Am I allowed to speak?” You’re asking “What exactly is expected from me, according to the rubric?”
claim_review_spans.R5: **Script you can send (short, polite, non-defensive):**
claim_review_spans.R6: > “Hi, can we confirm the presentation plan and grading? I saw my name on the slides task list, but I’m not sure if I’m also expected to speak. If speaking is required, could I have a small part (like 1–2 slides / my results) and I’ll practise that section?”
claim_review_spans.R7: If you’d rather do it in person, say:
claim_review_spans.R8: > “I want to make sure I’m contributing in the way the rubric expects. Are we assigning speaking parts, and can I do my results for the section I worked on?”
claim_review_spans.R9: - It gives you a “minimum safe” speaking role instead of an all-or-nothing situation.
claim_review_spans.R10: Instead of “I will speak” (which feels scary), ask for a role that reduces spontaneous speaking.
claim_review_spans.R11: Even if you end up mainly on slides, being ready to speak for 20–40 seconds is useful (in case of last-minute changes). The goal is not “perfect English”—it’s “clear English for the key points.”
claim_review_spans.R12: A simple template for your speaking part:
claim_review_spans.R13: 1) **What I did** (1 sentence)
claim_review_spans.R14: 2) **What I found** (1 sentence)
claim_review_spans.R15: 3) **Why it matters / difference from expected** (1 sentence)
claim_review_spans.R16: You mentioned you get stuck on three sentences—keep the same content, but make the words *more segmented* (shorter phrases, not one long sentence). Often that’s what makes fluency jump.
claim_review_spans.R17: You said they laughed, and you couldn’t tell what it was. Sometimes that laughter is actually about *something specific* (a mismatch in explanation, a timing issue, a misunderstanding), not your accent. But your brain will still associate the moment with “accent = the problem,” so you avoid speaking. That’s understandable—but it can cost you grades if speaking is expected.
claim_review_spans.R18: 1) Do you have to present in front of the class on the same day, or is it like a small internal group presentation?

claim_review_spans.R1: I’m really sorry—getting a first paper back with a low grade so early can feel *personal*, especially when you worked hard and English isn’t your first language. But based on what you’ve shared, it doesn’t sound like you “aren’t the kind of person” who can do university in English. It sounds like you’ve run into a **very common first-year, first-semester mismatch**: what the instructor means by “your own argument,” and how to use feedback to revise.
claim_review_spans.R2: Changing words from the readings does not always equal “your own argument” to professors. Often they mean things like:
claim_review_spans.R3: - Your paper needs a **clear claim** (what you’re arguing, in your own words).
claim_review_spans.R4: - You need **reasons + evidence organized to support that claim** (not just summary of sources).
claim_review_spans.R5: - You need **your stance**, not only what the readings say.
claim_review_spans.R6: So “isn’t that my own writing?” — you may have written in English, yes, but the *argument* (the idea/position and how you prove it) may still be too close to the readings or not explicit enough.
claim_review_spans.R7: Also: one grade is feedback, not a verdict about who you are or your ability. First-year papers often start lower everywhere, and international students often feel it more because everything is both academic and language-heavy.
claim_review_spans.R8: Dropping can be a reasonable *administrative* choice in some cases—but right now your mind is probably using the grade as evidence for a harsh conclusion: “I can’t do this.” That conclusion is understandable emotionally, but it’s not reliable.
claim_review_spans.R9: You don’t need to decide “drop vs don’t drop” today. A better next step is to get clarity on:
claim_review_spans.R10: - Whether you can get help early enough to improve quickly
claim_review_spans.R11: You shouldn’t write anything yet—just confirm which course it is, because that’s a concrete problem you can solve.
claim_review_spans.R12: **Do this now (5 minutes):**
claim_review_spans.R13: 1. Go to the assignment page and look for the **course name/code** at the top.
claim_review_spans.R14: 2. Check whether you have **multiple dashboards** (some platforms show upcoming assignments from all courses).
claim_review_spans.R15: 3. Open the assignment details and find:
claim_review_spans.R16: If you tell me what platform it is (Canvas? Blackboard? something else) and what the **course title/code** shows on that “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page, I can help you identify it quickly.
claim_review_spans.R17: That’s also common after a bad grade. Your brain goes into “perfection mode,” so nothing feels acceptable.
claim_review_spans.R18: A useful shift: **don’t try to write a perfect paper.** Try to write a *rough draft that contains the argument*—you can fix language after the idea is there.
claim_review_spans.R19: If you want, we can do a tiny “starter” together for the assignment due tomorrow:

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful and isolating—especially so early after arriving, when you’re already adjusting and trying to read social cues in a new language/culture. I also want to gently challenge one part: two classmates being “busy” isn’t enough evidence to conclude “they don’t want you around,” and mixed signals (memes, chatting near you, not explicitly inviting you) can have a lot of innocent explanations.
claim_review_spans.R2: - **You asked on the wrong days / wrong moment.** “Busy” is often just that they can’t do lunch *then*, not a personal rejection.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Group dynamics:** some people talk plans around others without thinking about whether it’s an invitation.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **They assume you’re okay alone / don’t want to bother you.** If you’re not joining conversations, they may not know you want to be included.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **Language/cue uncertainty:** they may not realize you’re unsure, or they may assume you’ll read between the lines.
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Memes can be friendly, not just polite.** People often do small friendly gestures even when they’re not ready for full invitations.
claim_review_spans.R7: Not yet. Based on what you wrote, the club is currently one of your best chances to build connections—it’s also where the “evidence” is mixed. Quitting now would remove your fastest opportunity to test whether you can belong there.
claim_review_spans.R8: A better goal than “stop trying” is: **make it easier for people to include you** with clearer, low-pressure invitations.
claim_review_spans.R9: Instead of waiting for someone to invite you, aim for **one direct but casual line** that doesn’t require them to “read your intention.”
claim_review_spans.R10: > “Hey, I’m trying to find something to do on Saturday. Are you going anywhere with the club or friends?”
claim_review_spans.R11: > “I’m going to grab coffee after this—want to come?”
claim_review_spans.R12: > “I’m new here—does anyone want to meet up on Saturday? Even just something small.”
claim_review_spans.R13: Then do something important: **choose a response window**. If nobody answers in, say, 24 hours, you send *one follow-up* or you try the same tone in person next time. You’re not “waiting for someone to notice you”; you’re initiating and then reading what happens.
claim_review_spans.R14: Unread doesn’t automatically mean “they think you’re desperate.” But it does mean you’re protecting yourself from rejection—and that protection is making you feel worse.
claim_review_spans.R15: - Then let it be awkward for a moment. That’s normal when you’re new.
claim_review_spans.R16: 1) When you asked people for lunch, did you say it in a super casual way (“Want to grab lunch sometime?”) or more specific (“today at 1?”)?
claim_review_spans.R17: 2) Roughly how many people were at the club gathering, and did you manage to speak to anyone briefly (even small talk)?
claim_review_spans.R18: If you answer those, I can suggest exactly what kind of invitation will feel most natural in your situation—and help you draft a message you can post that won’t make you feel exposed.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful—especially in a lab group where you’re already under pressure to understand everything *and* express it in English. From what you described, I think you’re dealing with two separate issues at once:
claim_review_spans.R2: 1) **You had a real communication moment** that didn’t go smoothly (accent/word-finding made things harder).
claim_review_spans.R3: 2) **You’re interpreting that moment as a decision about your “place” in the group** (“they decided I can’t speak / I should just avoid speaking”).
claim_review_spans.R4: It might be true, but it also might be a *misunderstanding or a lack of confidence from them*, not a permanent judgment about you.
claim_review_spans.R5: Even if the group mark is the same for everyone, **some rubrics still evaluate presentation components** (clarity, explanation, Q&A, etc.). So avoiding speaking doesn’t guarantee a better outcome—it could actually cost you points *and* make your next group harder.
claim_review_spans.R6: Here’s a script you can use (simple, non-confrontational):
claim_review_spans.R7: > “I felt nervous yesterday explaining. I can contribute—could I be responsible for a small part like explaining my method/result for 1–2 slides? If my English is unclear, please stop me and I’ll rephrase.”
claim_review_spans.R8: If they say yes, you get a speaking target. If they say no, you learn *why* (time, role expectations, rubric, confidence) and you can negotiate from there.
claim_review_spans.R9: It may have been about pronunciation—but it also could have been nervous laughter, not “mocking.” Either way, you don’t need to solve it emotionally right now. For the presentation, you only need to prevent the same failure mode:
claim_review_spans.R10: - **Don’t rely on spontaneous explanation.** Use a prepared “script” you can read closely.
claim_review_spans.R11: - **Use a speaking plan that matches your slides**, not your memory.
claim_review_spans.R12: For your part, make it **3 parts only**. Each part is 1–2 sentences, rehearsed *with your slides open*:

claim_review_spans.R14: 2. **What changed / what you found** (result)
claim_review_spans.R15: 3. **Why it matters** (1 key takeaway)
claim_review_spans.R16: If you keep getting stuck, it’s usually because you’re trying to say too much. Reduce it until you can deliver it smoothly.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes sense that you’re uncomfortable. In your place, it’s not “rudeness” to want basic clarity and respect—you’re dealing with a mismatch between what you *assumed* “make yourself at home” meant and what your housemates are actually doing. And right now you’re hungry + stressed, so it’s totally reasonable that you want a low-conflict way to handle it.
claim_review_spans.R2: Also: you’re not necessarily “difficult.” Many cultures differ on sharing, but you still get to set boundaries—especially when it’s about *your food* and privacy.
claim_review_spans.R3: You need two things: (1) get food without conflict, (2) signal a boundary without a big argument.
claim_review_spans.R4: - If you have your own food upstairs: eat that.
claim_review_spans.R5: - If not, you can do a short “excuse” to get what you need:
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Script:** “Sorry—I haven’t eaten yet. I’m going to grab something from the fridge real quick.”
claim_review_spans.R7: This isn’t rude; it’s just letting them know you’re doing something normal.
claim_review_spans.R8: If they offer takeaway again, you can accept without accepting the “your food is shared” rule:
claim_review_spans.R9: Don’t try to do a deep explanation while friends are in the kitchen. Do it when it’s just you + housemates (or at least when it’s quieter).
claim_review_spans.R10: - “From now on I’ll label my stuff, and if you want any, just ask first, please.”
claim_review_spans.R11: This avoids blaming them for culture; it states your preference and creates a clear method.
claim_review_spans.R12: What you’re noticing (“make yourself at home” + then strangers using your things) is exactly why you need *a specific rule*, not a cultural guess. Boundaries can be:
claim_review_spans.R13: - “If you want to share, let’s agree on common food vs my personal stuff.”
claim_review_spans.R14: You actually don’t need to have already said “that’s my food” to deserve respect now. But it will make things easier to say it clearly once—then you won’t have to keep hiding upstairs.
claim_review_spans.R15: When they used your food, did you see *who* took it (or was it unclear), and are your housemates generally friendly when you speak normally with them?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really lonely and confusing—especially so early after arriving and when you *are* making an effort. I also hear a lot of pain in what you’re concluding (“they obviously don’t want me around,” “if I stop trying I won’t look desperate”). Two quick things can be true at once: (1) it’s possible those specific classmates were genuinely busy, and (2) you’re still getting strong signals of exclusion in the *way* you’ve experienced things.
claim_review_spans.R2: I wouldn’t say “there isn’t much point going to the club again” yet. Based on what you described, the bigger issue looks like **unclear invitations + you feeling like any attempt will expose you**, so you retreat before people have a chance to include you.
claim_review_spans.R3: - “Busy” two times = not necessarily rejection. People often avoid planning with new people even if they’re friendly, because it feels risky/awkward.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Talking about Saturday right next to you = they might assume you aren’t interested, or they forgot you need an explicit invite.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Memes from one person = that can be politeness *or* a small bridge—they’re at least comfortable interacting with you.
claim_review_spans.R6: None of this proves “they don’t want you around.” It proves you haven’t yet had a clear, low-pressure moment where someone includes you directly.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Step 1 (today/next club meeting): make a small, specific invitation**
claim_review_spans.R8: You can message or say something like:
claim_review_spans.R9: - “Hey, are you going to anything this Saturday? I’m free—want to join?”
claim_review_spans.R10: - “I’m going to get food after the meeting. Anyone wants to come?”
claim_review_spans.R11: Specific + low stakes = easier for people to say yes.
claim_review_spans.R12: **Step 2: don’t rely on group-chat guessing**
claim_review_spans.R13: Group chats often move fast and people may not read/notice everyone. Instead:
claim_review_spans.R14: - After sending a message, if it’s unread, follow up in person if you see someone.
claim_review_spans.R15: - Or reply directly to someone who *is* active in the chat: “You said you’re free on Saturday—what are you thinking?”
claim_review_spans.R16: **Step 3: go for a short time, but stay for one interaction**
claim_review_spans.R17: If staying only 10 minutes feels like “proving you tried,” you can make it more effective:
claim_review_spans.R18: - Go for the usual time (or 20–30 minutes),
claim_review_spans.R19: - Pick **one** person you’ll talk to for 2 minutes (not “make friends,” just talk).
claim_review_spans.R20: Unread messages aren’t automatically a social rejection. People can be busy, distracted, or forget to check chat.
claim_review_spans.R21: If you feel embarrassed, here’s a better tactic than stopping:
claim_review_spans.R22: - If no one answers, you still use the next meeting to approach one person directly.
claim_review_spans.R23: > “There isn’t much point going to the club again, right?”
claim_review_spans.R24: I’d rephrase: **“There might be some point, but you should change the way you try—not stop trying.”** Right now, you’re trying in a way that requires other people to read your mind and include you. Changing to a clearer, smaller invitation usually gets better results.
claim_review_spans.R25: When you sent those group chat messages, what did you say exactly (roughly)?
claim_review_spans.R26: If you paste 1–2 of them (you can remove personal details), I can help rewrite them so they’re more likely to get a reply and feel natural for your voice.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful—especially in a lab group where you *already* feel under pressure and then your message doesn’t come out the way you planned. And it makes sense your brain feels “tired” after speaking English all day; fatigue can hit hardest right when you need confidence and quick words.
claim_review_spans.R2: 1) **Their reaction doesn’t automatically mean you “can’t speak.”** People laugh for lots of reasons (awkwardness, surprise, not knowing what to say), and repeating “what?” can be about *clarity and speed* more than ability.
claim_review_spans.R3: 2) **Task assignment isn’t the same as the final grading decision.** Your teammates are giving you guesses (“same group mark” vs “speaking marked separately”). The truth will be whatever the rubric and instructor say.
claim_review_spans.R4: 3) **Practicing only three sentences can trap you.** If you freeze when you get stuck, you end up running the same rehearsed lines instead of building a flexible explanation.
claim_review_spans.R5: Ask for a quick check so you’re not deciding based on teammate assumptions.
claim_review_spans.R6: **Option A (best): email/message your TA/professor**

claim_review_spans.R8: Our group presentation is coming up soon. I’m an international student and sometimes struggle with clarity when speaking quickly in English. I wanted to ask: **is there a speaking component that’s graded separately from the group content**, and is there a rubric I can review? claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really uncomfortable—especially because you already said “maybe,” and now it’s turned into people being in your shared space and using your food. Your feelings make sense, and you’re not “difficult” for wanting basic clarity and boundaries. What’s happening is mostly a communication mismatch: you were being polite, but you didn’t get to set the terms.
claim_review_spans.R2: Also: you *don’t* need to “accuse” anyone to protect your space. You just need simple, specific rules.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Get food that’s yours without entering the kitchen right now.** If you have any safe backup (snacks, instant food, bottled drink), use that.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **If you have to use the kitchen:** wait until there’s a lull and then go in with a neutral script (below). You don’t have to justify yourself—just do what you need.
claim_review_spans.R5: Your goal is to make it factual and low-drama: *“I need X.”* Here are a few ready-to-use lines.
claim_review_spans.R6: - “Hey—just a headspring for me. Could we keep visitors to **agreed times**? I’m still settling in.”
claim_review_spans.R7: - “I’m okay with visitors sometimes, but can we please **message me first** before friends come over?”
claim_review_spans.R8: This addresses the real issue (timing/permission) without discussing their culture.
claim_review_spans.R9: You can keep it very simple:
claim_review_spans.R10: - “By the way, that food is **mine**. Could you please not use my groceries?”
claim_review_spans.R11: - “I’m using my own groceries—can we keep them separate?”
claim_review_spans.R12: If you want even softer wording:

claim_review_spans.R14: - “I’m just about to eat—then I’ll go back to my room for a bit. No worries.”
claim_review_spans.R15: 1) Eat somehow (even if it’s just something quick).

claim_review_spans.R17: **Soon (next time they’re calm, not during visitors):**
claim_review_spans.R18: - “I want to be clear about my food—please don’t use my groceries unless I say it’s okay. Also, for visitors, could we agree first so it’s not awkward for me?”
claim_review_spans.R19: That’s it. No long apology, no debate about culture.
claim_review_spans.R20: Right now, you’re acting like “they’ll understand the unstated rule.” You don’t need to guess anymore. In shared living situations, it’s normal to say clearly what you’re comfortable with—especially in the first weeks of settling in.

claim_review_spans.R1: I’m really sorry—getting a first paper back as a brand-new student can feel like the whole “I belong here” question gets decided in one number. That 48 is painful, especially when you already spent a lot of time. But based on what you shared, I don’t think this is a sign you “can’t do university in English.” It sounds much more like you’re hitting a normal transition problem: understanding what *your professor means by “your own argument”* and how to format that in a first-year assignment style.
claim_review_spans.R2: If you rewrote/paraphrased readings into your own sentences, that *is* your own writing. So your confusion is valid. What feedback like “needs your own argument” usually means something slightly different, like one (or more) of these:
claim_review_spans.R3: - You may have summarized sources but didn’t clearly state a specific stance (what you think) and prove it.
claim_review_spans.R4: - Your points may not have been organized around a clear claim (the “argument”), even if the sentences were your own.
claim_review_spans.R5: - Your paragraphs may have “supported information” but not connected back to a central thesis.
claim_review_spans.R6: - You might still be too close to the structure/wording of the reading (not plagiarizing necessarily—just not yet showing your *analysis*).
claim_review_spans.R7: So: the feedback is about **thinking/structure**, not your ability to write English or your worth as a student.
claim_review_spans.R8: Think of your first paper like a baseline. You’ve learned something concrete already:
claim_review_spans.R9: - and that you need a clearer thesis/argument structure.
claim_review_spans.R10: That’s fixable. Plenty of students get their first mark back before they fully understand the “game” of university writing. It’s not “you vs. English”—it’s learning the genre and expectations.
claim_review_spans.R11: Right now your brain is overloaded because you’re not sure which class/assignment is due. You don’t need more anxiety—you need one clear check.
claim_review_spans.R12: **Can you open the assignment page and tell me the exact class name/course code shown at the top of the page?**
claim_review_spans.R13: Once I know that, I can help you determine whether it’s the same class as the 48-mark paper or the other one, and what the next best step is.
claim_review_spans.R14: Dropping can be a sensible choice sometimes—but it should be based on information, not panic. Since you’re already thinking “another load of questions would make my head worse,” I suggest a *tiny* decision-step:
claim_review_spans.R15: **Do not decide to drop yet.** Take one step that gives you information within 20–30 minutes:
claim_review_spans.R16: 1) confirm which course has “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.”
claim_review_spans.R17: 2) skim the assignment prompt for that course and identify: **(a) thesis/argument requirement** and **(b) format/length**.
claim_review_spans.R18: Then you’ll be deciding with facts, not fear.
claim_review_spans.R19: From what you wrote: you are not wrong to feel hurt, but you *are* wrong to conclude “I’m not the kind of person who can do university in English” based on one grade and one piece of feedback. The “own argument” comment is normal and teachable.
claim_review_spans.R20: Reply with the **course name/code** shown on the “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.” page, and I’ll help you figure out what you should do next (and how to start writing without everything feeling “wrong”).

claim_review_spans.R3: - Some people are awkward with new students and don’t know how to include you yet.

claim_review_spans.R5: - Unread messages in a group chat don’t necessarily mean rejection; it can mean people check at different times, or they don’t want to reply while they’re in the middle of plans.
claim_review_spans.R6: I wouldn’t jump to that conclusion yet. claim_review_spans.R8: > “Hi, I’m new here—do you want to get coffee before the next meeting? It can be quick.”

claim_review_spans.R3: - The laughter likely felt personal, but laughter in group settings is often messy/awkward (people sometimes laugh at misunderstanding, stress, or the tension of communication—not necessarily at your value). Still, it’s valid that it hurt.
claim_review_spans.R4: - You’re getting mixed messages about how group work is marked. That means the **rubric/assessment method** matters a lot before you decide what to do.

claim_review_spans.R6: You can do this in a quick message to the teammate who seems most involved, or to the lab leader/TA if you have that contact.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Option A: message a teammate (short)**

claim_review_spans.R9: > “I’m practicing the explanation, but I get stuck when presenting. Would it be possible for me to speak for a small section (like explaining what I did / one slide) and keep the rest slide-only?”
claim_review_spans.R10: If you tell me **who you can contact** (lab leader/TA vs teammate) and whether you have the presentation title/topic, I can tailor the exact wording.
claim_review_spans.R11: Given what you wrote, I’d recommend you **ask for a speaking part**, but **make it small and specific**. Reason: you’re already practicing, and you don’t want this moment to accidentally become a long-term pattern (“quiet student = no speaking”).
claim_review_spans.R12: - You prepare the slides (you’re already doing that),

claim_review_spans.R15: Until you know the grading:

claim_review_spans.R3: **“I’m hungry—does anyone have something I can eat quickly?”**
claim_review_spans.R4: This avoids going into the kitchen while they’re there and also keeps it neutral.
claim_review_spans.R5: - If you have anything sealed (snack, instant food, takeaway voucher, etc.), use that for now. Then you deal with the communication when they’re calmer.
claim_review_spans.R6: **Option C (if you can’t eat): ask for a quick time**
claim_review_spans.R7: **“Sorry—just today I’m tired and I need quiet. Can you let me use the kitchen after your friends leave?”**
claim_review_spans.R8: You need to set two boundaries gently:
claim_review_spans.R9: 1) **Visitors:** whether guests are allowed and when
claim_review_spans.R10: 2) **Personal items/food:** what is yours, and what you’re okay sharing
claim_review_spans.R11: - **“Hey, just so I understand—are friends okay in the kitchen like this? I’m a bit unsure about the routine here.”**
claim_review_spans.R12: - **“Could you ask me first next time? I’m still adjusting and I need to plan.”**
claim_review_spans.R13: - **“Thank you, but I actually bought that food for myself—could you check with me next time before using my stuff?”**
claim_review_spans.R14: - **“I’m not finished—would you mind keeping my items separate?”**

I can’t tell you that you’re “not wrong” about dropping it, because I don’t yet know what the assignment was really testing or what the class expectations are. But I *can* say this:

claim_review_spans.R3: - you summarized sources instead of taking a clear stance,
claim_review_spans.R4: - your “argument” wasn’t explicit (or didn’t stay consistent),
claim_review_spans.R5: - your points weren’t organized to prove a thesis.
claim_review_spans.R6: Also, “needs your own argument” often appears when a student has used sources/changed wording, but the *structure of thinking* isn’t yet “yours” in the way the rubric means. claim_review_spans.R7: You can absolutely write in your own words and still be missing what the grader means by “your own argument.” For example, you might have:

claim_review_spans.R9: So your wording may be original, while your *argument* is still too close to the readings or too indirect.
claim_review_spans.R10: This part is a very concrete problem, not a “you can’t do it” problem. Confusion here can happen easily when you’re new and juggling multiple class sites.

claim_review_spans.R15: I hear that dropping feels “sensible.” That feeling makes sense when you’re overwhelmed. But dropping is usually an irreversible response to something that might be fixable with one targeted improvement.
claim_review_spans.R16: A compromise that protects you without committing to dropping immediately is:

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really lonely—especially because it happened right after you arrived, and you’re trying to do the “right” things (inviting lunch, showing up to club events) but it doesn’t feel like you’re getting a clear opening back.
claim_review_spans.R2: A few things that might be going on (none of this means you’re “unwanted”):
claim_review_spans.R3: - **“Busy” is not always “no.”** People often default to busy when they’re awkward, distracted, or don’t know you well yet.
claim_review_spans.R4: - **The club planning thing sounds ambiguous, not hostile.** If they were talking right beside you, they may have assumed you didn’t need the info, or they just forgot to include you in the moment.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **Unread group chat messages can become a self-fulfilling spiral.** Not because you’re wrong to feel awkward—but because once you start believing “they don’t want me here,” it becomes harder to read what’s actually happening.
claim_review_spans.R6: - **Memes = partial connection.** Even if it’s “polite,” it’s still a real bridge. Polite can turn into friendly if you give it structure.
claim_review_spans.R7: So to your question—**no, I wouldn’t say there’s “no point” going to the club again.** I’d call it a “wrong strategy, not wrong person” situation. The missing piece is usually *how* you approach and *what kind* of invitation you make, not whether you should try.
claim_review_spans.R8: **Goal:** make it easy for people to include you without putting you in the position of “waiting to be noticed.”
claim_review_spans.R9: 1) **Go once more, and choose one concrete role**
claim_review_spans.R10: - People are more likely to respond to *tasks* and *time-based plans* than to a vague social invitation.
claim_review_spans.R11: 2) **Use a “specific yes/no” invite (instead of lunch + open-ended)**
claim_review_spans.R12: - “Hey, I’m going to get food after this—want to join?”
claim_review_spans.R13: - “What are you doing Saturday? I’m free in the afternoon; want to join me?”
claim_review_spans.R14: 3) **If you posted in the group chat, follow up with a short message that includes you in the plan**
claim_review_spans.R15: - “Hi everyone—I'm new here and still figuring out Saturday. Is anyone going to the club activity / doing something fun? If so, I’d love to join.”
claim_review_spans.R16: 4) **Don’t interpret “not invited directly” as rejection**
claim_review_spans.R17: - Instead interpret it as: *you haven’t created a clear invitation channel yet.*
claim_review_spans.R18: You can send something like:
claim_review_spans.R19: - “Hey! I’m trying to make plans for Saturday—anyone want to go together? Totally okay if not.”

claim_review_spans.R7: Because you only need **$200**, you don’t necessarily need a whole job—small bridging works.

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds really painful—especially in a lab group where you *need* to contribute clearly. And it also sounds like you’re not actually failing at the work; you’re getting hit by the two hardest things at once: (1) English pressure in real time and (2) feeling judged when you couldn’t explain yourself.
claim_review_spans.R2: - **Your accent/language can be the trigger, but it doesn’t automatically mean you “can’t speak.”** In early group work, people often react awkwardly when someone struggles—then it becomes a social moment. That doesn’t equal your ability.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **Getting put next to “preparing slides” doesn’t have to be permanent.** It may reflect a safe default for them, or it may be how the group handled the last meeting. You can renegotiate before the presentation.
claim_review_spans.R4: For this presentation, you can aim for **a speaking role that is small, prepared, and low-risk**, rather than “perfect speaking” or “no speaking.”
claim_review_spans.R5: - **You speak for 30–60 seconds** (or one slide / one section), using **a script you can read from**
claim_review_spans.R6: - You don’t improvise. You practice *reading + delivery*.
claim_review_spans.R7: **Step 1 (now, 20 minutes):** Decide the smallest speaking role that still feels like “mine.”
claim_review_spans.R8: - “I will explain Slide 3 (the result difference) in ~45 seconds.”
claim_review_spans.R9: - “I will say the conclusion + one key number from my result.”
claim_review_spans.R10: - “I will read the methods step for my part of the lab.”
claim_review_spans.R11: **Step 2 (next 30–60 minutes):** Write a script that’s *not 3 sentences stuck in your head*.
claim_review_spans.R12: Use 5–7 short lines. Example template (customize to your slides):
claim_review_spans.R13: > “In my experiment, the results were different because of [reason].
claim_review_spans.R14: > Step [X] affects [variable].
claim_review_spans.R15: > The expected value was [X], but we observed [Y].
claim_review_spans.R16: > This leads to the interpretation that [main meaning].
claim_review_spans.R17: > In conclusion, the difference comes from [one phrase].”
claim_review_spans.R18: - reading it aloud slowly 5 times,
claim_review_spans.R19: - then once with a timer (even if you don’t hit perfect timing yet).
claim_review_spans.R20: **Step 3 (before the presentation):** Ask for the speaking part in a low-pressure way.
claim_review_spans.R21: You don’t need a debate about the rubric. You can frame it as helping the team run smoothly.
claim_review_spans.R23: > “I want to contribute to the speaking part. For the presentation, could I speak for just my section—like explaining Slide [X]—about one minute? I’ll have a script.”
claim_review_spans.R24: If they say “everyone gets the same mark,” you can respond:
claim_review_spans.R25: > “Great—then I’ll take my one-minute part so everyone hears the result clearly.”
claim_review_spans.R26: If they say speaking is separate:
claim_review_spans.R27: > “Then I want to do my best for my portion. I can speak from the slide notes so it’s clear.”
claim_review_spans.R28: Given what happened yesterday, I’d recommend **a speaking role that is small and scripted**—not because you “must prove yourself,” but because:
claim_review_spans.R29: - speaking practice under real conditions is how you’ll build confidence,
claim_review_spans.R30: - and your group is already labeling you as “non-speaker” based on one difficult moment.
claim_review_spans.R31: You can start small so you don’t feel exposed, while still changing the pattern.
claim_review_spans.R32: Even if their laughter was about your accent, it still doesn’t automatically mean they’ll be fair or supportive about your contributions. Their behavior was unkind/awkward. You’re allowed to take control of how you participate.
claim_review_spans.R33: 1) What is your presentation section—**what do you need to explain** (methods, the “result difference,” analysis, or conclusion)?
claim_review_spans.R34: 2) About how long is your part supposed to be—**30 seconds, 1 minute, or 3+ minutes**?
claim_review_spans.R35: If you paste the slide title(s) or the exact “result difference” sentence you’re trying to say, I can help you turn it into a short, easy-to-deliver script.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes a lot of sense that you feel stuck. You tried to be polite the way you were taught, but because you said “yeah maybe” (without clarifying), your housemates treated your answer as permission. Now the real problem isn’t just the visitors—it’s that you didn’t get to set clear boundaries *and* you’re dealing with hunger at the same time.
claim_review_spans.R2: A gentle truth: there’s no single “correct culture.” In shared living, “make yourself at home” usually means *“we’re friendly”*—but it still should come with clarity about what is shared vs. private. What you’re experiencing is common for international students: you’re being respectful, but your needs weren’t communicated.
claim_review_spans.R3: 1) **Text/call a housemate quietly (or speak to one person, not the group):**
claim_review_spans.R4: “Sorry—I'm hungry and I need to eat before things get busy. Are you using the kitchen right now? I’m going to get my food from the fridge/pantry.”
claim_review_spans.R5: 2) **Go get your own food quickly, even if they’re there:**
claim_review_spans.R6: If your food is identifiable, bring it out with you and eat at a different place in the house (your room, desk area). This signals “this is mine” without a big conversation.
claim_review_spans.R7: If you want, tell me: do you have *some* identifiable food (your name on it / a specific shelf / container), or is it mixed in communal areas? That changes what wording is safest.
claim_review_spans.R8: Your goal is: **clear future rules + explain your perspective briefly + ask what they prefer.**
claim_review_spans.R9: You can say something like:
claim_review_spans.R10: > “I want to check something—my food was in my place, so I was surprised it got used. In the future, can we keep personal food separate? If people want food, they can ask me first.”
claim_review_spans.R11: > “I’m okay with sharing in some situations, but I need to be clear about personal items. Next time, could you ask before using my food?”
claim_review_spans.R12: **Option C (if you don’t want to mention “my food” directly):**
claim_review_spans.R13: > “I’m still adjusting to house rules. For food, should we treat it as shared by default, or is personal food private? I’m a bit confused.”
claim_review_spans.R14: Notice: you’re not accusing anyone of “being wrong.” You’re setting a rule going forward.
claim_review_spans.R15: No—you don’t have to be “rude.” You just need *neutral clarity*. For next time, instead of “yeah maybe,” you can use language that protects you:
claim_review_spans.R16: - “**I’m not sure yet—ask me later.**”
claim_review_spans.R17: - “**I’m not comfortable with visitors in the kitchen—can we do it at a different time?**”
claim_review_spans.R18: - “**Let me check first, I’m keeping things private today.**”
claim_review_spans.R19: Right now, you don’t actually have to prove they stole from you. You just need to say:
claim_review_spans.R20: - “I didn’t realize you’d take it as permission.”
claim_review_spans.R21: When you say “some food I bought has been used”—was it **clearly in your space** (your shelf/fridge compartment), or was it in a **shared/kitchen area**?

claim_review_spans.R1: That sounds *really* painful—especially because it’s your first semester abroad, your first time writing in English in a university setting, and you already invested a lot of time. I can see why a 48 would keep replaying in your head.
claim_review_spans.R2: But I don’t want to agree with the part that “one bad mark means you’re not the kind of person who can do university.” That conclusion is coming from fear, not evidence.
claim_review_spans.R3: This specific wording usually does **not** mean “you didn’t write your own words.” It more often means something like:
claim_review_spans.R4: - or your paragraphs stayed too close to the sources (summarizing) without turning that into your own claim,
claim_review_spans.R5: - or you didn’t explain *why* your evidence supports your claim,
claim_review_spans.R6: Also, rewriting from readings can still be “your writing” linguistically—professors may still feel the *thinking* is not yet yours in the way they need. That’s fixable.
claim_review_spans.R7: It makes sense you feel frozen when the deadline is “tomorrow at 5 p.m.” and you’re not sure which course it belongs to. When your brain is already stressed, details like “which class?” feel like they can break you.
claim_review_spans.R8: Open your course management system (Canvas / Blackboard / whatever you use) and do this for **the assignment page that says “submit tomorrow at 5 p.m.”**:
claim_review_spans.R9: 1. Click the assignment title (or assignment details) and look for the **course name/code** displayed at the top.
claim_review_spans.R10: 2. Also check whether there’s a **due date/time zone** shown there.
claim_review_spans.R11: 3. If you can’t immediately find it, look at your **To-Do / Calendar** for tomorrow—does it list which class the submission is for?
claim_review_spans.R12: If you tell me the **exact course name/code** shown on that assignment page (just that text), I can help you figure out the fastest way to proceed.
claim_review_spans.R13: Dropping can be a sensible option sometimes—but right now it sounds like you’re considering it from a place of overload and shame (“my head is worse,” “I’m not that kind of person”). That’s not the same as making a calm choice based on workload, grades, and support.
claim_review_spans.R14: So instead of deciding “drop vs don’t drop” today, I’d suggest a *trial approach*:
claim_review_spans.R15: - get the deadline sorted,
claim_review_spans.R16: - then decide after you see what you can do with help/feedback.
claim_review_spans.R17: You are not wrong to take feedback seriously. But you *are* probably jumping to an extreme meaning from it. Many first-year students—especially when English is not their first language—get early marks that look scary while their underlying academic skills are still developing. This is exactly the stage where feedback is meant to teach you how the system expects arguments.

claim_review_spans.R1: It makes total sense that you feel discouraged. From your side, it’s not just “making friends takes time”—it’s *two direct lunch rejections*, plus standing near conversations where it’s unclear whether you’re being included, plus your club messages not getting replies. That combination can make you feel like you’re being avoided, even if other explanations are possible.
claim_review_spans.R2: I can’t know their motives, but I do think your conclusion (“there isn’t much point going to the club again”) is stronger than the evidence you actually have.
claim_review_spans.R3: - **They’re genuinely busy / distracted** that day (busy schedules are common in the first semester).
claim_review_spans.R4: - **You may be reading “private plans” risk onto everything**—they might have been talking about what the club is doing Saturday, but you couldn’t read the cues.
claim_review_spans.R5: - **Group dynamics:** sometimes people assume “someone else will invite,” especially in mixed groups. Not inviting you directly doesn’t automatically mean “we don’t want you around.”
claim_review_spans.R6: - **The meme person:** sending memes can be real connection, not just politeness—but even politeness is still engagement. It suggests they notice you.
claim_review_spans.R7: And also: **unread messages doesn’t necessarily mean rejection.** Group chat messages often get ignored because people are multitasking, in class, asleep, or they’re waiting to respond in the moment they’re free.
claim_review_spans.R8: If you go to the club and keep trying in a *slightly different way*, you’re not “desperate”; you’re doing the normal work of socializing. The difference is: instead of messages that might get overlooked, you switch to a **low-pressure, specific ask** in the moment.
claim_review_spans.R9: 1) **Fast inclusion move**
claim_review_spans.R10: > “Hi, I’m new here—what are you guys planning to do on Saturday? Is it connected to the club?”
claim_review_spans.R11: 2) **Direct but low-stakes invite**
claim_review_spans.R12: > “I’m going to grab food after this—want to join? If not, no worries.”
claim_review_spans.R13: 3) **Follow-up without sounding demanding**
claim_review_spans.R14: > “Sorry I missed the plan—should I come to the next meeting or is Saturday something separate?”
claim_review_spans.R15: These remove the ambiguity you mentioned (whether Saturday is club activity or private plans). People find it easier to respond to something *specific*.
claim_review_spans.R16: I’d say **don’t stop yet**—at least not based only on two lunch “busy” answers and unread messages.
claim_review_spans.R17: - If that second attempt clearly results in consistent dismissal or rudeness (not just “busy”), then you reassess and choose another way to meet people (another club, study group, dorm event, language exchange, etc.).
claim_review_spans.R18: You said: “If I stop trying, at least I won’t look desperate.”
claim_review_spans.R19: But in practice, the “desperate” risk is usually *in how you pressure people*, not in how often you reach out. Asking one clear, friendly question is normal—especially for a newcomer.
claim_review_spans.R20: When you sent messages in the club group chat, did you ask something *specific* (e.g., “What time are we meeting Saturday?”) or was it more general (“Anyone going?” / “Hi”)?
